title: Your morning

lines: AN ALARM, A THUMB, A SCREEN.
WHO OWNS THE FIRST TEN MINUTES?
cards: How does your morning start now? On plenty of mornings it goes like this: an alarm, a thumb on a screen, the news, a group chat, somebody else's emergency, all before feet touch the floor.
On a morning like that, the first ten minutes belong to whoever reached the phone first.

This week you've collected the pieces of something else: not a new obligation, a different first ten minutes, built from parts you already know. Today i put them together, in order, and hand them to you.

teach.b: Here's a shape built from those parts, close to what some Buddhists do at home, with many variations. One: the bow. At your quiet corner, or just beside the bed, three bows: Buddha, dhamma, sangha.
Pride set down before the day picks it up. Two: homage. Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa, three times, turning the mind in one direction.
Some people add the three refuges and the five precepts here, taking them fresh each day. If you'd like, light the candle, offer a flower.
Three: the breath. Sit, and let the breath be known, long as long, short as short, the way you learned in the breathing weeks. Five minutes is plenty.
Four: metta. The four phrases: may you be safe, may you be happy, may you be healthy, may you live with ease. Start with yourself, then widen, to someone you'll see today, to everyone.
Five: dedication. Whatever good came from these minutes, may it be shared.
Then one word, said three times: sadhu, sadhu, sadhu. Good, well done. People say it at the end of a chant, a talk, a gift.

It means: I rejoice in this. Look back and the whole week is here: the homage, the quiet corner, a Buddha on the shelf, flowers that fade, light and scent, the shared merit, now in order. Ten minutes.
Nothing about it requires you to be calm first, or to feel spiritual. The shape is there on the mornings when nothing in you feels like it.

how: Some Buddhists begin the day at a home shrine with bows, the homage chant, the refuges and precepts, a short sitting, loving-kindness and a dedication of merit, often closing with 'sadhu' three times.

o: a short daily practice before the day begins
a monk's long dawn chant in the temple hall
an early start to get more work done

games.q: match the step of the morning to what it does.
p: pride set down before the day starts
turns the mind in one direction
may you be safe, may you be at ease
well done: I rejoice in this

s: you have to feel calm before a morning practice can work
the shape is there on the mornings when nothing in you feels like it.
sadhu means 'good, well done' and is said three times
people say it at the end of a chant, a talk or a gift.
the morning practice gathers pieces from this week and earlier weeks
bow, homage, breath, metta and dedication, all learned before.

games.q: you've done the bow, the homage and the breath. what comes next in the morning's shape?
o: the five precepts, a second time.
games.why: metta follows the breath, then the dedication of merit, and the morning closes with sadhu, sadhu, sadhu.

practice: Lower your head once, gently, and turn the mind toward what you value. Let the breath come and go and simply know it; then, may I be safe, may I be at ease, may everyone I meet today be at ease.
Whatever good came from this, may it be shared, and if you like, say sadhu, quietly, three times.

wordCard.voice: Your morning. Bow, homage, breath, metta, dedication: ten minutes that belong to you before the day begins.

orig.note: Pali: good, well done; said three times to rejoice at the end of a chant, a talk or a gift.

carryVoice: Your line: a morning, yours. Ten minutes, before anyone else gets them. Day one hundred forty-four, done.
